_readme: Canned results for Tracey's data tools — one entry per tool name, shaped like the DIGEST that
tool really returns (see frontend/src/features/tracey/tools/*.ts, the `store(kind, full, digest)`
second argument). Only the digest reaches the model, so that is all a fixture needs.
These describe one small, coherent project — the kiosk demo world — so a multi-tool turn stays
self-consistent: the agent ids here appear in the runs, the runs in the case results, and so on.
A tool with no entry answers 'call succeeded, no data' and is flagged in the report; add an entry
when a scenario needs that tool to have something to say. Scenarios can override any of these.
navigate / load_skill / search_docs are never stubbed — they run for real.
An entry may ECHO THE CALL back the way a real API does, which matters most for writes and for
by-id reads: a model that posts a correction and reads back `isCorrection: false`, or that probes
two suites and gets the same one twice, concludes its own correct call did not land and burns the
step budget re-doing it — a harness artifact that reads in the report as a prompt regression.
The vocabulary (resolved by scripts/fixture-world.mjs) is:
{ "_byArg": "suiteId", "_cases": { "<id>": … }, "_default": … }  pick a branch by an argument;
with no branch and no _default the answer is `{ notFound: <value> }`, exactly what the real
by-id tools return for an id the project does not have.
{ "_forEach": "cases", "_item": …, "_empty": … }  one entry per element of an array argument.
{ "_like": "get_suite", …overrides }  start from another entry (resolved against the same
arguments) and override keys on top of it — one suite body, not five copies of it.
"$args.x" / "$item" / "$item.x" — a value from the arguments or the current _forEach element.
"$has.args.x" / "$has.item.x" — was it sent? "$count.args.x" — length of an array argument.
"$index", "$uuid" — position, and a stable minted id (same call ⇒ same id, so an A/B diff is
never noise). Keys starting with `_` are dropped, so `_comment` works anywhere.
Known simplifications, so a reader does not mistake them for the product: compare_runs pins its
pass rates to the world's one real before/after regardless of which run ids it is handed;
add_to_suite / remove_test_case return the suite as it stood BEFORE the write (only `addedCases`
is derived from the call) and never report `unpassableCases`; get_case_results answers `fail` for
the freshly started run and `pass` for the A/B candidate run whatever case is asked about, which
is what makes the test-driven-improvement red→green loop reachable here.

_writes: Write tools echo the call so a curation / optimization flow can run to the end on results that
agree with what was posted. `_like: "get_suite"` reuses the suite bodies above, so a write
against a suite the world does not have answers `{ notFound }` — which is what the real tools do,
since each looks the entity up before mutating.
`awaitable` handles matter: they are what makes the model call await_actions next, as in the app.

addedCases._comment: Same _forEach path as `cases`, so $uuid mints the same id for the same case — addedCases[i].caseId is cases[i].id, as in the app.

set_suite_evaluators._comment: The whole set is replaced, so the answer must be exactly the ids that were sent — a silently reduced set is what makes a model retry the write until it runs out of steps.

start_test_run._comment: 5, not 4: the world assumes the refund suite just gained the case a scenario added — which is what await_actions and get_case_results then report on.

await_actions._comment: One result per handle, dispatched on the handle's own kind — a wait batching a run and a theory must answer about both, not about whichever the fixture happened to name.
